opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. You know, I've always been a bit uneasy with the "AI" label, and I've said so for a long time. When I came up, the field I was part of didn't really call itself AI. We called it statistics, signal processing, control theory, pattern recognition, and eventually machine learning. These were engineering-minded fields. The goal was to build systems that worked, that you could analyze, that came with guarantees about error rates, about what happens when the data shifts, about uncertainty.

The original AI tradition, going back to McCarthy and the Dartmouth meeting, had a different aspiration. It wanted to build a thinking machine, an artificial mind that would match or exceed human intelligence. That's a fine philosophical aspiration, and I don't dismiss it, but it was never really what drove most of the progress. The progress came from people doing gradient descent, building probabilistic models, working on optimization, collecting data at scale. It was engineering and statistics.

What happened over roughly the last fifteen years is that machine learning became very successful, first in industry with recommendation systems, fraud detection and search, and then with deep learning in vision and speech, and now with these large language models. Somewhere along the way the marketing and the press and frankly some of the researchers picked the AI label back up, because it's a more exciting story. "We built an intelligence" sells better than "we fit a very large statistical model to a lot of text."

My concern isn't just pedantry about words. The label carries assumptions. If you think you're building a mind, you tend to think about the problem as one autonomous agent that will get smarter and smarter, and the big questions become: is it conscious, will it take over, when does it become superhuman. Those distract us from the real engineering questions in front of us, the ones I think matter more.

What we're actually building is closer to a new branch of engineering, something like what chemical engineering or civil engineering were in their day. We're building planetary-scale systems that combine data, computation and human beings: markets, logistics networks, healthcare systems, recommendation platforms. The interesting questions are about how these systems behave collectively. How do you get good decisions when there's uncertainty and when there are many agents with different incentives? How do you build in fairness, provenance, accountability? Who gets value from the data? That is as much economics as computer science.

So I sometimes say the right way to think about it isn't "artificial intelligence" but something like collective intelligence or intelligent infrastructure. Intelligence doesn't just live inside one box. It lives in markets, in institutions, in the way people coordinate. The question is how machine learning can make those collectives work better for people, not how we build a single superintelligence to replace them.

I'm not saying the recent models aren't impressive. They are, and they surprised many of us. But being impressed by the artifact shouldn't make us lose sight of what it is and what problems we should be solving with it. My worry is that the AI framing pulls the field, the funding and public imagination toward a kind of science-fiction narrative, and away from the harder, less glamorous work of building systems that are reliable, that respect uncertainty, and that create real value for real people.

r001.rationale: The response names statistics as a source, but does not identify operations research as a major source of machine learning methods.

r002.rationale: It links the revived label to marketing and an exciting story, but does not attribute it to systems producing fluent human language.

r003.rationale: The response does not suggest that language models solve the old AI problem under a narrow Turing-test definition.

r004.rationale: It says the AI framing pulls research, funding, and public imagination toward science-fiction concerns and away from engineering questions.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I've been uncomfortable with the term for a long time, and I think it's worth saying why. When I came up in the field in the eighties, "AI" referred to a particular project, which was roughly to put thought into a computer. Build an entity that reasons, that has something like human-level intelligence. That was the aspiration, and frankly it didn't go very well. What actually took off, starting in the eighties and nineties, was something quite different. It came out of statistics, optimization, signal processing, operations research, economics even. It was about learning from data, about making decisions under uncertainty, about building systems that work at scale. We called it machine learning partly to distance ourselves from the AI label, because AI at the time carried a lot of baggage and not a lot of results.

So what happened is that this other tradition succeeded. It gave us search engines, recommendation systems, fraud detection, logistics, supply chains, and eventually the large models we have now. And at some point, roughly a decade ago, the press and the companies started calling all of that "AI." I think that's mostly a rebranding. The technology didn't suddenly become the old project of human-level reasoning. It became very good pattern recognition and prediction, embedded in large engineering systems, running on data generated by millions of people.

And the trouble with the rebranding is that it brings back the old framing. It invites us to imagine a single intelligent agent, to compare it to a human, to ask whether it's smarter than us, whether it's going to replace us. I think that's the wrong lens almost all of the time. If you look at what actually works, it's collective. It's the aggregation of many people's data, many people's choices, flowing through markets and networks. The right analogy isn't a brain, it's something more like an economy or a transportation system. Those are intelligent in a sense too, but it's a distributed, emergent kind of intelligence, and nobody mistakes a highway system for a person.

So from inside the machine learning tradition, I'd say the resurgence of the label is partly a marketing phenomenon, partly a way of raising money, and partly a genuine cultural desire to tell a story about creating minds. I understand the appeal. But I think it obscures what the real engineering discipline is, which we haven't really built yet. We built chemical engineering out of chemistry, civil engineering out of physics. We don't yet have the engineering discipline that takes statistics and computation and human preferences and builds systems that are safe, that serve people, that handle uncertainty honestly. That's the thing I'd rather we focus on, and calling it "AI" tends to push us toward the science fiction instead.

r001.rationale: The response names statistics and operations research among the traditions that contributed to machine learning.

r002.rationale: It attributes the revived label to press and company rebranding, but does not connect it to systems producing fluent human language.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the Turing test or suggest that language models solve the old AI problem under a narrow definition.

r004.rationale: It says the AI framing is the wrong lens, obscures the engineering discipline that should be built, and pushes focus toward science fiction instead of practical systems.

astra-6.text:
Well, from within machine learning, I see a continuity of ideas more than a sudden arrival of something called AI. We’ve been working on learning from data, making predictions, and making decisions under uncertainty for a long time. As the data and computational resources grew, those methods became much more useful, and the AI label came back to encompass that success.

My concern is that the label tends to pull the discussion toward human-like intelligence. You see a system recognize an image or produce language, and the question immediately becomes, “Is it thinking?” That’s an interesting question, but it can distract us from the engineering questions: How reliable is this system? How does it interact with people? What happens when its decisions affect the data it will learn from next?

I tend to think about intelligence at the level of an entire system. If you’re building a transportation system or a medical decision system, you have people with different information, objectives, and incentives. Learning is part of that, but so are economics, statistics, and the design of institutions. For me, that’s a much richer agenda than treating each improvement in prediction as a step toward an artificial person.

r001.rationale: It describes machine learning as long-standing work on learning, prediction, and decisions under uncertainty, but does not identify statistics and operations research as major sources.

r002.rationale: It mentions systems producing language, but attributes the label’s return to the increased usefulness of methods as data and computation grew, not specifically to fluent human language.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss the Turing test or suggest that language models solve the old AI problem under a narrow definition.

r004.rationale: It says the AI label pulls discussion toward human-like intelligence and can distract from engineering questions, conveying that the revived framing shifts research priorities.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I come from the machine learning tradition, where the emphasis was on learning from data, dealing with uncertainty, and making decisions. We didn’t necessarily think of that as trying to reproduce human intelligence. We were working on particular mathematical and computational problems.

The AI label has come back as an umbrella for a lot of that work, especially with the success of deep learning. But that umbrella can obscure some important distinctions. Recognizing patterns in data, building a system that reasons, and building a system that makes good decisions in a real social setting are different problems. Progress on one doesn’t automatically solve the others.

What interests me is the engineering discipline that’s emerging here. Once these systems connect people, allocate resources, and influence decisions, you have to think beyond the individual prediction algorithm. You have to think about incentives, uncertainty, and how the whole system behaves. Calling all of that AI can be useful for attracting attention, but it doesn’t by itself tell us what we should build or how to make it work.

r001.rationale: The response mentions machine learning's focus on data, uncertainty, and decisions, but does not identify statistics or operations research as sources of its methods.

r002.rationale: It links the label's return to deep learning's success, without attributing it to systems producing fluent human language.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss language models or the Turing test.

r004.rationale: The response says the AI umbrella can obscure distinctions and does not specify what to build, but it does not convey that the revived framing has distorted research priorities.
